what_happened.summary: That moment stings, and it's worth talking about. Whether those pitches were strikes was the umpire's call; what the player controls is readiness, where he stands, and his approach. This guidance comes from draft coaching notes that haven't been reviewed yet.

output.call_type_rationale: The umpire's judgment decides what happened; a written rule then sets what follows.

channel.how: Let your child talk first on the ride home and keep it supportive; ask the coach for a few minutes later in the week if you want to talk technique.

output.teachable_moment: A game built on failure: In baseball, succeeding about 30% of the time at the plate can make a Hall of Fame career at the professional level. That's a 70% failure rate. You will not win every competition, and you will not lose every competition, but you will learn and grow through every competition.

individual: Before the at-bat, set your feet so the end of the bat covers the far edge of the plate. If the pitcher keeps missing away, inch closer.
Pick one thing to work on (for example, plate coverage or the two-strike approach), practise it this week, and let the rest go.
team: Tee: two-strike outside corner: From a tee on the outer half, hitters take a slightly shorter two-strike swing and drive the ball the other way. Five quality reps, then switch. Safety: Set the net so missed balls cannot reach a walkway. Helmet on for every swing.
at_home: Remind your child that even the best hitters fail most of the time. A tough day is part of the game, not a sign they don't belong.

life_lesson.text: Failing often on the way to success is normal in anything worth doing; what matters is learning from each try.

lessons.title: A game built on failure
lessons.principle: In baseball, succeeding about 30% of the time at the plate can make a Hall of Fame career at the professional level. That's a 70% failure rate. You will not win every competition, and you will not lose every competition, but you will learn and grow through every competition.

lessons.title: Believe in your players before they believe in themselves
lessons.principle: Have confidence in your players even when they don't show it, even when their track record says failure. Don't lose that confidence. Feed it to them and they will succeed.

recalled.content: A coach of a 12-year-old baseball player asked: My 12U pitcher threw 68 pitches Friday. Can she pitch Sunday?
